prompt.1: Food, gas and rent cost more now. What should the government's plan be?
prompt.2: Groceries, gas and rent cost more than they used to. Which approach should the province take?
prompt.3: Which approach should the province take on the cost of living?
prompt.4: Which cost-of-living approach should come first: tax cuts, price rules, more help for low incomes, or targeted credits and rate caps?
prompt.5: Which mix of cost-of-living measures should the province put first: broad tax cuts, price controls, income support, or targeted credits and rate caps?

context.1: Prices for food, gas and rent have gone up. Every party says it wants to make life cost less. Some want to cut taxes. Some want rules that keep prices down. Some want more help for people with low incomes.
context.2: Prices were 2.9% higher in July 2026 than a year before. Every party promises to make life more affordable, but they disagree on how. The province could cut taxes for everyone, limit some prices, give more money to people with the lowest incomes, or lower costs for businesses so they can charge less.
context.3: Cost of living is the top issue for BC voters. In 2025 the NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax, but it paused a $1,000 rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest tax rate. Every party promises relief in a different way. Some would cut income taxes for everyone. One would cap markups on gas and some groceries. Another would raise support for the poorest people. Others mix smaller tax cuts with limits on power and car insurance increases.
context.4: Cost of living ranks first for 56% of BC voters, according to an Ipsos poll. The minimum wage is $18.25 an hour and rises with inflation each year. In 2025 the NDP government paused a $1,000 grocery rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest income tax rate. The parties' price tags are hard to compare. The Conservative and OneBC tax cuts have no published cost. The Greens have not published how they estimated their wealth tax revenue, and CentreBC's cost figures are its own, not checked by anyone else.
context.5: Consumer prices rose 2.9% in the year to July 2026. The NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax in April 2025, and Budget 2026 raised the lowest income tax rate from 5.06% to 5.60%. The NDP proposes a 10-cent-a-litre fuel tax cut with a BC Utilities Commission cap on gas margins, caps on grocery margins, and a freeze on Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (ICBC) rates. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount, the income you earn tax-free, to $32,000. The Greens would raise income assistance to the poverty line and make transit free for people under 25 and over 65. CentreBC would return the lowest rate to 5.06%, raise the renter's credit to $600 and cap BC Hydro and ICBC increases. OneBC would cut every income tax rate by 25% and the provincial sales tax (PST) by two points.

text.1: This party would let people earn more before paying income tax, and it promises no new taxes.
text.3: The Conservatives promise to raise the tax-free amount to $32,000 (about $1,000 a year), add no new taxes while in government, and remove provincial sales tax from Canadian alcohol until the trade conflict ends. The party has not costed it; an NDP candidate calls it a $2.5 billion hole and economist Ross Hickey estimates about $2 billion a year. It would reverse the 2026 change to the Property Tax Deferment Program, which moved taxes deferred from 2026 on from simple interest at prime minus 2% to prime plus 2% compounded monthly. It voted against the 2026 bill (Bill 2) that raised the lowest rate.

scoring_rationale: Option a is the OneBC 25% cut and PST reduction (4); Conservatives share a broad cut but at a different scale and have not endorsed rate cuts of that size (2); CentreBC 1 (cuts one bracket modestly inside a legislated balance path and rejects cuts of this size); NDP and Green 0. Option b is the Conservative basic personal amount increase (4); OneBC 3 (would cut everyone's taxes, by a different instrument); CentreBC 2 (a broad income tax cut, but through the bottom rate, about half the size, and costed); NDP 1 (it did cut MSP and the carbon tax, but its 2026 direction is price regulation and a higher bottom rate); Green 0. Option c is the NDP 2026 package (4); Greens would require margin disclosure and set limits where margins are excessive, but have no fuel tax cut or ICBC freeze (2); CentreBC 2 (caps Hydro and ICBC increases, a Crown-rate measure, but no grocery caps or fuel tax cut); Conservatives oppose price regulation but kept their own targeted PST-off-alcohol measure (1); OneBC 0. Option d is the Green plan (4); NDP 2 because it indexed the minimum wage and expanded benefits but froze child care and has no assistance pledge; CentreBC 1 (renter's credit and a caregiver benefit, no assistance or wage pledge, no wealth tax); Conservative and OneBC 0 (a non-refundable credit gives nothing to the lowest incomes). Option e is CentreBC's platform package (4): bottom rate to 5.06%, renter's credit $600, commuter credit, Hydro and ICBC caps, PST machinery relief; Conservatives 3 (voted against the bottom-rate rise, no new taxes, machinery PST exemption; no renter or rate-cap measures); OneBC 2 (broad tax cuts, no targeted measures); NDP 1 (it created the renter's credit and the ICBC freeze but enacted the rate rise the option reverses); Green 1 (renter support only). Option e was rewritten on October 10 from the earlier farm PST item, which the platform does not repeat; other parties' scores on it were kept. Symmetry check: Conservative on a (2) and OneBC on b (3) are within one point; NDP on e (1) and CentreBC on c (2) are within one point.

prompt.1: The province spends more money than it takes in. What should it do?
prompt.2: BC spends more than it takes in. What should it do?
prompt.3: BC expects to spend about $13.8 billion more than it takes in this year. What should it do?
prompt.4: Which path should BC take on its deficit: tax cuts, taxing high incomes or wealth, spending restraint, or continued borrowing?
prompt.5: Which approach to taxes, spending and borrowing do you support for BC's $13.8 billion deficit?

context.1: The province spends more money than it takes in, so it borrows the rest. Borrowing costs extra because of interest. The province could spend less, raise some taxes, or keep borrowing.
context.2: BC expects a deficit of about $13.8 billion this year, which means it spends that much more than it takes in. It borrows to cover the gap, and that adds interest costs. It can spend less, tax some people more, keep borrowing until the economy grows, or mix these.
context.3: BC's deficit, the gap between what it spends and what it takes in, is about $13.8 billion. That is a record in dollars. All four credit rating agencies lowered BC's rating in 2026. No party has a fully costed plan, so the parties' promises and price tags are hard to compare.
context.4: BC now forecasts a $13.8 billion deficit this year, up from $13.3 billion in Budget 2026, and debt rising to 37% of gross domestic product (GDP), the size of BC's economy, by 2028-29. The parties' plans differ in size. The NDP's higher tax on high incomes would raise about $1 billion a year. The Conservatives have not costed their tax cut; an economist puts it at about $2 billion a year. The Greens estimate their wealth tax would raise $22.2 billion in its first year. CentreBC says its promises cost $13.7 billion over four years and would balance the budget in 2034-35. OneBC has not costed its cuts.
context.5: Budget 2026 projected a $13.3 billion deficit for 2026-27, and the September quarterly update raised the forecast to $13.8 billion. Taxpayer-supported debt is projected to reach 37.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2028-29, and all four credit rating agencies downgraded BC this year. The NDP would add two points to the top two income tax brackets and charge 24.5% above $1 million (about $1 billion a year), and plans 15,000 fewer full-time-equivalent public positions. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount to $32,000 (not costed by the party; an economist puts it at about $2 billion a year and an NDP candidate at $2.5 billion) and set no deficit target. The Greens would tax wealth above $50 million ($22.2 billion in year one, party estimate). CentreBC would write a 2034-35 balanced budget into law, cut 10,000 positions as people leave and return the lowest rate to 5.06% (its tax relief costs $4.5 billion over four years, party costing). OneBC would cut taxes 25% and balance in four years.

scoring_rationale: Five options give each party a clear home. a = OneBC (4); Conservatives share deep tax cuts but have no balance date (2); CentreBC shares a legislated balance target but on an eight-year path with a modest cut (1). b = Conservative 2026 position (4); OneBC close (3); CentreBC 2 (a bracket cut, but a legislated balance date and party costing, which the option lacks); NDP and Green 0. c = CentreBC's platform (4): balance 2034/35 in law, Independent Budget Officer, attrition, bottom rate to 5.06%; Conservative 2 (fiscal rhetoric without a balance date or costing); NDP 1 because it enacted the bottom-rate increase the option reverses and has no balance date, although its fiscal plan also cuts FTEs; Green 1; OneBC 1 (a balance date, but four years and 25% cuts). d = NDP record and platform (4), including the enacted Budget 2026 measures; Green 2 because it voted for Supply 2025 but voted against the Budget 2026 bill at both readings and calls the NDP's top-bracket increase 'not very effective' next to its wealth tax (score changed Oct 13 after source check); CentreBC 1 (also protects front-line services and cuts positions by attrition, but rejects the deficit path and the bracket increases). e = Green (4); NDP 1 for the school tax increase above $3M and top brackets, but it has adopted none of the option's instruments (wealth levy, windfall tax, royalty reform); others 0. The NDP-Green cross-scores are asymmetric on purpose: the Greens voted for the NDP's 2025 supply bill but against Budget 2026 (2 on d), while the NDP has taken up none of the Green instruments (1 on e). Record over rhetoric: the NDP is scored on its enacted budget path, not only its campaign framing; the Conservatives are scored as uncosted because the 2024 balance pledge has been dropped. Symmetry: Conservative on a (2) and OneBC on b (3) are within one point.
